analysis.one_liner: Narrows agencies' power to keep business records secret from the public.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2019 by four senators split evenly between the parties, the bill went to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tighten one of the government's main excuses for keeping records secret under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). It says a company's information given to a federal agency can only be withheld from the public if releasing it would likely cause the company substantial competitive harm — a much stricter standard than agencies have often used. It also stops agencies from hiding parts of a record by claiming those parts don't match the request, and reaffirms that agencies may not refuse to give records to Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who files a FOIA request: journalists, watchdog groups, researchers, and ordinary citizens seeking information about how agencies regulate companies — from safety data to contract and trade records. Congress also gains a clearer right to records.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Journalists, watchdogs, and citizens requesting records

how_it_helps.text: Redefines 'confidential' business information so it can be withheld only if release would likely cause substantial harm to the company's competitive position, closing a route agencies have used to withhold records about regulated businesses.
Bars agencies from splitting a responsive record and refusing to release portions merely by labeling them 'non-responsive', a tactic that hides material a requester is entitled to see.
Restates that FOIA is not authority to withhold information from Congress, preserving legislative oversight of agency record-keeping.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that hand confidential commercial data to federal agencies — drug makers submitting applications, contractors, importers in trade cases — would face a higher bar for keeping that information out of public view, and genuine trade secrets could become available to competitors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Firms submitting confidential business data to agencies

drawbacks.text: The strongest objection: the strict 'substantial competitive harm' standard could expose genuinely valuable trade secrets that companies share with regulators, such as proprietary formulas, pricing data, or manufacturing details, to their competitors.
If firms fear their submissions will become public, they may be more reluctant to cooperate candidly with agencies, which could reduce the quality of information regulators use to protect consumers.
The change codifies a standard courts have already largely applied to this FOIA exemption, so it is a modest fix rather than a broad overhaul of government secrecy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but diffuse: FOIA releases let reporters and citizens see how agencies treat regulated companies, which underpins accountability. The costs fall on a narrower group — businesses with legitimately sensitive data on file with agencies — and courts already require some competitive harm before withholding, so the bill narrows the shield rather than eliminating it. A modest, well-aimed transparency improvement with manageable costs; the main problem with it is not its design but that no one acted on it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there; the committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Grassley introduced the bill on July 23, 2019 with three other senators from both parties — Patrick Leahy, John Cornyn, and Dianne Feinstein — as original sponsors.
That same day the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary; that referral was the last action of any kind in the entire Congress.
The bill never reached the Senate floor, never received a committee or floor vote, and expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agencies and the regulated companies that rely on the broad trade-secrets exemption came out ahead: the wider authority to withhold business records from FOIA requesters, journalists, and Congress remains untouched, and the committee that declined to act faced no vote or roll call on the issue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and companies relying on broad secrecy rules

sides.party_line_note: The bill had balanced bipartisan sponsorship from the start — original sponsors Grassley (R) and Cornyn (R) with Leahy (D) and Feinstein (D) — and there is no record of anyone opposing it; it simply never advanced in a Republican-controlled committee and Senate.

industries.industry: Regulated companies and government contractors submitting confidential business data to federal agencies
industries.note: The bill would raise the bar for withholding their commercial information from FOIA disclosure, so pricing, application, and trade data on file with agencies could become public. Their interest in secrecy runs against the public's interest in seeing how agencies treat regulated firms, though some protection for genuine trade secrets is a legitimate concern.
A narrower secrecy exemption and a bar on 'non-responsive' partial withholdings would make more agency records obtainable, directly serving the watchdog role these groups play for the public.
